title: Service Manager Salary: Hourly to Annual Conversion with Casual Loading and Super
description: Convert your service manager salary from hourly to annual using 38-hour weeks. Includes casual loading, super paid on top, and tax estimates from Fair Work data.
salarySummary: A service manager earning $50 per hour on a 38-hour week would have an annual gross salary of $98,800 before super and tax.

faqs.q: What is the typical service manager salary in Australia?
faqs.a: Service manager salaries vary by industry and experience. The Fair Work Ombudsman pay guides set minimum award rates for classifications like managerial roles, but many service managers earn above award. As a reference, the Australian Bureau of Statistics reported full-time adult average weekly ordinary time earnings of $2,083.70 in May 2026, which equates to about $108,352 annually. Your actual service manager salary may be higher or lower depending on your award or agreement.

faqs.q: How does casual loading affect my service manager salary?
faqs.a: If you work as a casual service manager, you are entitled to a 25% loading on top of the base hourly rate. For example, if your base rate is $50 per hour, the casual rate becomes $62.50 per hour. This loading compensates for not receiving paid leave entitlements. The Fair Work Commission sets the casual loading at 25% of the national minimum wage, and it applies to award-covered employees. Always check your award or agreement for specific rules.

faqs.q: Is superannuation included in my service manager salary?
faqs.a: No, superannuation is paid on top of your salary. From 1 July 2026, the super guarantee is 12% of your ordinary earnings, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830. For a service manager earning $100,000 annually, the employer must contribute an additional $12,000 into your super fund. This is not deducted from your pay; it is an extra benefit. Use the timesheet tool to see your total remuneration including super.

bodyMarkdown:
## Understanding the Service Manager Salary

If you are negotiating a **service manager salary** or evaluating a job offer, knowing how to convert an hourly rate to an annual figure is essential. In Australia, most full-time roles are based on a 38-hour week, and the standard formula is:

**Annual gross salary = hourly rate × hours per week × 52**

For example, a service manager earning $50 per hour working 38 hours each week would have an annual salary of $50 × 38 × 52 = $98,800. This is before tax, superannuation, and any deductions.

But your actual pay may include casual loading, penalty rates, or allowances. The Fair Work Ombudsman provides [pay guides](/blog) for each modern award, which set minimum rates for classifications including managerial roles. If you are award-free, the National Minimum Wage applies: from 1 July 2026, it is $26.44 per hour or $1,004.90 per week for 38 hours. A service manager salary is typically well above this minimum.

## How to Convert Hourly to Annual

To convert your hourly rate to an annual salary, multiply by the number of hours you work each week and then by 52 weeks. The [the timesheet](/) tool on this site does this calculation for you. It assumes a consistent 38-hour week unless you adjust it. If you work part-time or irregular hours, adjust the weekly hours accordingly.

### Fortnightly Pay

Many employers pay fortnightly. Your fortnightly gross pay is simply your weekly pay multiplied by two. For a $50 per hour service manager on 38 hours, weekly pay is $1,900, so fortnightly pay is $3,800 before tax and super.

### Award Rates vs Market Rates

The Fair Work Commission’s Modern Awards Pay Database contains minimum rates for each classification. A service manager may be covered by the Managers Award or a specific industry award. However, market rates for experienced service managers often exceed award minimums. The Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) Average Weekly Earnings for May 2026 show full-time adult ordinary time earnings of $2,083.70 per week, or about $108,352 annually. This is a useful benchmark for a typical service manager salary.

## The Role of Casual Loading

If you work as a casual service manager, you are entitled to a 25% loading on top of your base hourly rate. This is set by the Fair Work Commission and applies to most modern awards. The loading compensates for not receiving paid sick leave, annual leave, or public holiday pay.

For example, if your base hourly rate is $50, the casual rate becomes $62.50 per hour. Your annual salary as a casual would then be $62.50 × 38 × 52 = $123,500. However, this higher rate does not include super; super is still paid on top of the casual rate.

**Important:** When using the timesheet tool, never enter a rate that already includes casual loading. Instead, enter your base hourly rate and check the “Add 25% casual loading” box. The tool will calculate the loaded rate for you.

## Superannuation Paid on Top

Superannuation is a mandatory employer contribution, not a deduction from your salary. From 1 July 2026, the super guarantee is 12% of your ordinary time earnings, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830. This means if your service manager salary is $100,000, your employer must pay an additional $12,000 into your super fund.

Super is calculated on your ordinary earnings, which include your base salary and any loadings like casual loading, but exclude overtime. The [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging) page explains how salary packaging can affect your super contributions.

### Example with Super

For a permanent full-time service manager earning $50 per hour ($98,800 annually):
- Super contribution: 12% × $98,800 = $11,856
- Total remuneration: $98,800 + $11,856 = $110,656

For a casual service manager at the same base rate ($62.50 loaded):
- Annual ordinary earnings: $123,500
- Super: 12% × $123,500 = $14,820 (still within the $270,830 cap)
- Total remuneration: $123,500 + $14,820 = $138,320

## Tax Considerations

Your take-home pay depends on tax withheld. The 2026–27 resident tax rates are:
- Nil on income up to $18,200
- 15% on income from $18,201 to $45,000
- 30% on income from $45,001 to $135,000
- 37% on income from $135,001 to $190,000
- 45% on income above $190,000

Plus a Medicare levy of 2% (with possible reductions for low-income earners). For a service manager earning $98,800, the estimated tax (including Medicare) would be around $22,267, leaving a take-home pay of about $76,533 annually or $1,472 per week. Use the [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) page for a more detailed estimate.

## Using the Timesheet Tool

The [the timesheet](/) tool on this site is designed for exactly this purpose. Enter your base hourly rate, select your hours per week (default 38), and check the casual loading box if applicable. The tool will show your annual gross salary, fortnightly pay, estimated super, and approximate tax. It uses the latest Fair Work and ATO figures.

Remember, this is an estimate. Your actual service manager salary may include allowances, penalty rates, or salary sacrifice arrangements not captured here. Always refer to your award or employment contract for precise terms.

### Summary of Key Figures

- National Minimum Wage (from 1 July 2026): $26.44/hour, $1,004.90/week for 38 hours
- Casual loading: 25% on top of base rate
- Super guarantee: 12% of ordinary earnings, paid on top, capped at $270,830
- ABS Average Weekly Earnings (May 2026): $2,083.70/week full-time adult ordinary time

By understanding these components, you can confidently evaluate any service manager salary offer and plan your finances.
